title: User Error
description: User Error is the 2007 album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of alternative metal about designing technology for the people who actually use it. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Qword plays lead guitar, Wyrd moves to piano and atmospheric synths, and Bytes plays drums and sings backup. Affordances, mental models, feedback, user research, paper prototypes, think-aloud testing, Fitts’s law, memory limits, accessibility, dark patterns and undo. The title is ironic: the album argues there is no such thing as user error, only design error. The first pressing came in packaging nobody could open, which the band admits proved the point. Play loud. Watch your users.
tagline: The 2007 alt-metal album from Procedural Byts: a human-computer interaction course in twelve songs, and why it was never the user’s fault.
lineup: The four-piece, now user-tested. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Qword plays lead guitar. Wyrd plays piano and atmospheric synths. Bytes plays drums and sings backup.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, and the one who said there is no such thing as user error. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass, and she won the argument.

members.name: Qword
members.bio: Sixty-four bits and still soloing. Qword wrote the Fitts’s Law solo with big targets close together and has never missed it live.

members.name: Wyrd
members.bio: Thirty-two bits, on piano and atmospheric synths, and the designer of the band’s paper prototypes, drawn on index cards. Three cards were thrown away. The site works.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, drums and backing vocals. He said “user error” once, in 2007, and has been apologizing ever since, mostly by playing the drums for one person at a time.

members.name: Null
members.bio: Sat beside every usability test participant. Made them feel less judged. Has never once blamed the user.

story.heading: No Such Thing
paragraphs: In 2007 the band redesigned its fan site, and nobody could find the tour dates. Bytes said it was user error. Nyble said there is no such thing: if a fan can’t find the tour dates, the site failed the fan. The argument lasted a week, and it became an album.

Before writing a single song, the band spent a week answering fan mail by phone, just to hear how people actually used the site. Then Wyrd redrew the whole thing on index cards and tested it with fans before anyone wrote a line of code.

They ran a real usability test, too. Five fans were asked to buy a concert ticket while saying everything they were thinking. All five failed. One bought a T-shirt by accident. Two found the duck page and stayed there. Null sat beside every participant during the test, and several said it made them feel less judged, which has always been the duck’s whole job.

Then a fan wrote to say the site read the tour dates to her screen reader as “image, image, image.” The band rebuilt the site so every image had words, every video had captions, and everything worked from a keyboard. Accessible to All is for her.

The first pressing of the album came in a clever fold-out case that nobody could figure out how to open. Fans sent it back. The band admits it proved the point better than any song on the record. The second pressing has a tab that says “pull here.”

cover_sub: The 2007 album. There’s no such thing.

songs.title: User Error

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: They couldn’t find the button, so you said that they were slow,
They clicked the wrong thing twice, so you said they didn’t know.
But if a hundred people trip on the same step every day,
It isn’t all the people, it’s the stair that’s in the way!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: There’s no such thing as user error! (Design error!)
There’s no such thing as user error! (Look again!)
If they can’t use it, then it doesn’t work, no matter what you meant,
User error, user error, is an alibi you invent!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Design it for the people, not the people for the screen,
Watch them where they stumble and fix the space between.
User-centered from the start, and test it as you go,
The users aren’t the problem, they’re the ones who let you know!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: It’s not your fault! (It’s the design!)
It’s not your fault! (Draw a better line!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s solo trips over the same awkward phrase three times, in the same place. On the fourth pass, instead of practicing harder, Qword rewrites the phrase, and it flows.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: There’s no such thing as user error! (Design error!)
There’s no such thing as user error! (Look again!)
If they can’t use it, then it doesn’t work, no matter what you meant,
User error, user error, is an alibi you invent!

songs.note: Bytes said “user error” once, in 2007. This song is Nyble’s reply.
songs.lesson: Human-computer interaction is about designing technology around the people who use it. When many people make the same mistake, the problem is the design, not “user error.” User-centered design involves real users from the start: understanding what they need, designing, testing with them, and improving it again and again.

songs.title: Affordance

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A handle says to pull it and a flat plate says to push,
A button asks for pressing and a slider asks to rush.
The shape tells you the action before you read a word,
The affordance is the promise, and the signifier’s heard!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Affordance! (What it lets me do!)
Signifier! (Showing me the clue!)
If I have to read a sign that says to push it, it’s a lie,
Affordance, affordance, and the shape will tell me why!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A door with a handle that you’re meant to push will fool you every day,
And the sign that says to push it is the door that’s gone astray.
Make the right thing easy and the wrong thing hard to find,
A good design is obvious and leaves no doubt behind!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Push! (It says pull!) Pull! (It says push!)
A Norman door! (And everyone’s ambushed!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Every phrase in Nyble’s solo tells you where the next one is going before it gets there, so the band always knows exactly when to come back in. Nobody needs a sign.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Affordance! (What it lets me do!)
Signifier! (Showing me the clue!)
If I have to read a sign that says to push it, it’s a lie,
Affordance, affordance, and the shape will tell me why!

songs.note: The studio door had a big handle but could only be pushed. Everyone pulled it, every day, for six weeks.
songs.lesson: An affordance is what an object lets you do: a handle affords pulling, a flat plate affords pushing. A signifier is the visible cue that tells you so. Good design makes the right action obvious from the way things look. A door that needs a “push” sign because its handle says “pull” is called a Norman door, after Don Norman’s book The Design of Everyday Things.

songs.title: Mental Model

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I think it works like this, there’s a picture in my head,
The thermostat’s a faucet, so I crank it up instead.
The more I turn it, the faster it will heat, I say,
But it’s only on or off, and it heats the same old way!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Mental model! (What I think!)
Mental model! (On the brink!)
When my picture doesn’t match the way the system really runs,
Mental model, mental model, and the trouble has begun!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Show me how it works, and make the inside clear to see,
Map the controls to the things they change in front of me.
Four burners in a square and four knobs in a line,
Which knob is which? Arrange them like the burners, and it’s fine!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Consistent! (Same as before!)
Mapping! (Like it shows!)

parts.label: Piano solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd’s piano solo moves left when the melody goes down and right when it goes up, so you can follow it just by watching Wyrd’s hands. Then Wyrd crosses hands, and the band gets lost.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Mental model! (What I think!)
Mental model! (On the brink!)
When my picture doesn’t match the way the system really runs,
Mental model, mental model, and the trouble has begun!

songs.note: Bytes turned the studio thermostat all the way up every morning to make it warm faster. It never did.
songs.lesson: People build a mental model of how a system works, and when it doesn’t match how the system really works, they make mistakes, like cranking a thermostat all the way up thinking the room will heat faster. Designers should make the system’s workings clear, stay consistent, and use natural mapping, where controls are laid out like the things they control, such as stove knobs arranged like the burners.

songs.title: Feedback

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I pressed the button and nothing happened, so I pressed it nine more times,
Did it hear me? Is it working? There’s no sound and there’s no signs.
Ten orders went through, and now I’ve bought ten of the same,
Because nothing ever told me that the first one ever came!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Feedback! (Show me that you heard!)
Feedback! (Say a single word!)
A click, a light, a spinner, a bar that tells me how it goes,
Feedback, feedback, so everybody knows!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A tenth of a second feels instant, a second keeps me in the flow,
Ten seconds and I’m wandering, I need a bar to know.
Tell me what is happening and tell me what it did,
Keep the status visible, and never keep it hid!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Loading! (How long?) Saving! (Is it done?)
Tell me! (Tell me!) I’m not the only one!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Every phrase Qword plays gets an instant answer from the band, a hit, a chord, a fill, so Qword always knows it landed. Then for four bars the band goes silent, and Qword plays the same phrase over and over, louder and louder.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Feedback! (Show me that you heard!)
Feedback! (Say a single word!)
A click, a light, a spinner, a bar that tells me how it goes,
Feedback, feedback, so everybody knows!

songs.note: The studio’s tape machine had no light to show it was recording. Three songs were lost before anyone noticed.
songs.lesson: Feedback tells people their action was received and what happened. Keeping the system’s status visible is the first of Jakob Nielsen’s usability heuristics. Rough guidelines: a tenth of a second feels instant, one second keeps someone’s train of thought, and ten seconds is the limit of attention, so anything longer needs a progress indicator. Without feedback, people repeat actions and make mistakes.

songs.title: Know Your User

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I built it for myself because I know what I would do,
But I’m not the one who’s using it, and neither, friend, are you.
Go out and meet the people, watch them where they are,
Their goals, their work, their hands, their eyes, their kitchen and their car!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Know your user! (You are not the user!)
Know your user! (Go and meet them!)
Ask them what they need and watch them while they try,
Know your user, know your user, and you’ll understand why!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Write a persona, a person with a name and with a goal,
Somebody to design for, so you don’t lose control.
Interview and watch them, and listen more than speak,
The things they never say out loud are what you really seek!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Who are they? (Ask them!) What do they need? (Watch them!)
Where are they? (Go there!) What gets in the way? (Fix it!)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays the solo for one specific person in the front row, watching her the whole time, and changes the pattern every time she stops nodding. By the end she’s nodding on every beat.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Know your user! (You are not the user!)
Know your user! (Go and meet them!)
Ask them what they need and watch them while they try,
Know your user, know your user, and you’ll understand why!

songs.note: Before writing the album, the band spent a week answering fan mail by phone. Bytes still talks to two of the callers.
songs.lesson: “You are not the user”: designers’ own habits and preferences mislead them. User research, like interviews, observing people where they actually work, and studying their tasks, uncovers what people really need. Personas turn that research into a few realistic, named example users to design for.

songs.title: Paper Prototype

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Before you write the code, before you build a thing,
Draw it on some paper and see what the users bring.
A card for every screen and a sketch for every button,
Cheap to change and cheap to throw, it doesn’t cost you nothing!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Paper prototype! (Sketch it out!)
Paper prototype! (Test it out!)
Fail fast and fail cheap, before the code is set in stone,
Paper prototype, prototype, and you’re never on your own!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Low fidelity at first, the rough and quick and plain,
Then higher as you go, and test it all again.
Design and prototype and test, and learn from what you see,
Iterate the cycle till it’s what it ought to be!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Sketch! (Quick!) Test! (Watch!)
Learn! (Change!) And again! (Again!)

parts.label: Piano solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays a rough sketch of a melody, just the outline, then a slightly better one, then better again. Each pass takes four bars. By the fourth, the melody is finished, and it took less time than writing it carefully once.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Paper prototype! (Sketch it out!)
Paper prototype! (Test it out!)
Fail fast and fail cheap, before the code is set in stone,
Paper prototype, prototype, and you’re never on your own!

songs.note: Wyrd drew the band’s new website on index cards and tested it with fans before writing a line of code. Three cards were thrown away. The site works.
songs.lesson: Prototyping tests a design idea before you build it. Low-fidelity prototypes, like paper sketches and index cards, are fast and cheap to change, and people give more honest feedback on something that looks unfinished. Higher fidelity comes later. Design is a cycle: design, prototype, test, learn, and go around again.

songs.title: Think Aloud

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: Okay, I want a ticket… Tour, maybe? No…
What’s “Experience”? Why is there a duck here?

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Sit down and try to use it and say everything you think,
Every doubt and every guess, every pause and every blink.
I’ll sit beside you quiet and I won’t help you at all,
Your confusion is the data, and it’s writing on the wall!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Think aloud! (Say what’s in your head!)
Think aloud! (Every word you said!)
Five users find the most of what is broken, watch them try,
Think aloud, think aloud, and you’ll see the reason why!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Give them a real task, like buying a ticket to the show,
Watch them where they hesitate and where they want to go.
Don’t defend the design, don’t explain, and don’t lead,
Write down where they stumble, and that’s the fix you need!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Where would you click? (I don’t know!)
What do you expect? (It isn’t so!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays the solo like a first-time user: a phrase, a pause, a wrong turn, a step back, another try. You can hear every moment of confusion. The band writes them all down.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Think aloud! (Say what’s in your head!)
Think aloud! (Every word you said!)
Five users find the most of what is broken, watch them try,
Think aloud, think aloud, and you’ll see the reason why!

songs.note: The band asked five fans to buy a concert ticket on the website while saying everything they were thinking. All five failed. One bought a T-shirt by accident.
songs.lesson: In a think-aloud usability test, real users try realistic tasks while saying what they’re thinking. The observer doesn’t help, just notes where people hesitate, guess or get lost. Jakob Nielsen found that testing with about five users uncovers most of a design’s usability problems, so small, frequent tests work well.

songs.lyrics:
[Lineup: female lead vocals and bass guitar, lead electric guitar, piano and synths, drums with male backing vocals]

[Intro]
[Spoken Word: hesitant young voice, thinking aloud]
Okay, I want a ticket… Tour, maybe? No…
What’s “Experience”? Why is there a duck here?

[Verse 1: female lead vocal]
Sit down and try to use it and say everything you think,
Every doubt and every guess, every pause and every blink.
I’ll sit beside you quiet and I won’t help you at all,
Your confusion is the data, and it’s writing on the wall!

[Chorus: female lead vocal, male backing vocals]
Think aloud! (Say what’s in your head!)
Think aloud! (Every word you said!)
Five users find the most of what is broken, watch them try,
Think aloud, think aloud, and you’ll see the reason why!

[Verse 2: female lead vocal]
Give them a real task, like buying a ticket to the show,
Watch them where they hesitate and where they want to go.
Don’t defend the design, don’t explain, and don’t lead,
Write down where they stumble, and that’s the fix you need!

[Chorus: female lead vocal, male backing vocals]
Think aloud! (Say what’s in your head!)
Think aloud! (Every word you said!)
Five users find the most of what is broken, watch them try,
Think aloud, think aloud, and you’ll see the reason why!

[Bridge: female lead vocal, male backing vocals]
Where would you click? (I don’t know!)
What do you expect? (It isn’t so!)

[Lead Guitar Solo: hesitant searching phrases that pause, backtrack and try again before finding the way]

[Final Chorus: female lead vocal, male backing vocals]
Think aloud! (Say what’s in your head!)
Think aloud! (Every word you said!)
Five users find the most of what is broken, watch them try,
Think aloud, think aloud, and you’ll see the reason why!

[End]

songs.title: Fitts’s Law

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: How long will it take you to hit a target with your hand?
It depends how far away it is and how big it stands.
Small and far is slow, and big and close is fast,
Make the things that matter big and close, and they’ll be found at last!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Fitts’s law! (Big and near!)
Fitts’s law! (Make it clear!)
The distance and the size decide how long it takes to reach,
Fitts’s law, Fitts’s law, and that’s the lesson that we teach!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The corners of the screen are targets that you cannot miss,
The pointer stops right at the edge, there’s nothing bigger than this.
Keep the dangerous buttons far from the ones that are used the most,
Make the common actions big, and keep the common actions close!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Far and small! (Slow!)
Near and big! (Go!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword built the solo so every note is a big, easy target close to the last one. It’s fast, it sounds hard, and it never misses.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Fitts’s law! (Big and near!)
Fitts’s law! (Make it clear!)
The distance and the size decide how long it takes to reach,
Fitts’s law, Fitts’s law, and that’s the lesson that we teach!

songs.note: Qword wrote this solo with big targets close together. Qword has never missed it live.
songs.lesson: Fitts’s law (1954) predicts that the time to point at a target grows with how far away it is and shrinks with how big it is. Important and frequent targets should be big and close. The edges and corners of a screen are especially easy to hit, because the pointer stops there, which makes them effectively infinitely large.

songs.title: Seven, Plus or Minus Two

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Read me a number once and I’ll lose it by the door,
Short-term memory holds a handful, seven, maybe four.
Chunk it into groups and it’s easier to keep,
Don’t make me remember what you could show, it’s cheap!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Seven, plus or minus two! (That’s all I hold!)
Seven, plus or minus two! (Or so I’m told!)
Recognition beats recall, so show me what to choose,
Seven, plus or minus two, and the rest I’ll lose!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A menu shows me all the choices, I just have to see,
A command line makes me remember, and that’s harder on me.
Don’t make me think, don’t make me hold it in my head,
Every thing you show me is one less thing I dread!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Five, five, five! (Chunk it!)
One, two, one, two! (Easy!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble plays a twelve-note bass line that nobody in the band can remember. Then she plays it again in three chunks of four, with a breath between each, and the whole band plays it back perfectly.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Seven, plus or minus two! (That’s all I hold!)
Seven, plus or minus two! (Or so I’m told!)
Recognition beats recall, so show me what to choose,
Seven, plus or minus two, and the rest I’ll lose!

songs.note: The main riff is seven notes long. Nobody in the band could remember the original twelve-note version.
songs.lesson: Short-term (working) memory is small. George Miller’s famous 1956 paper said about seven items, plus or minus two; later research suggests closer to four chunks. Chunking, grouping things together like the parts of a phone number, helps them fit. Good design keeps memory load low: let people recognize options instead of recalling them, as a menu does, and keep needed information on the screen.

songs.title: Accessible to All

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: She hears the web instead of seeing it, a voice that reads the page,
But every picture without words is silence on the stage.
Give every image words and label every field,
And everyone can get inside, and nothing is concealed!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Accessible to all! (Everyone gets in!)
Accessible to all! (That’s where we begin!)
Design for the edges and the middle comes along,
Accessible to all, and everyone can sing the song!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Captions for the ones who can’t hear, and they help in noisy rooms,
Contrast you can read in sunlight, not just in the gloom.
Everything by keyboard for the ones who can’t use a mouse,
Build the ramp, and everybody walks into the house!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Can you hear it? (Captions!) Can you see it? (Contrast!)
Can you reach it? (Keyboard!) Built to last!

parts.label: Piano solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays the melody so it can be followed however you listen: once in the low register, once in the high, once as rhythm alone. Nobody needs to see Wyrd’s hands to know exactly what’s happening.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Accessible to all! (Everyone gets in!)
Accessible to all! (That’s where we begin!)
Design for the edges and the middle comes along,
Accessible to all, and everyone can sing the song!

songs.note: A fan wrote to say the band’s website read the tour dates to her screen reader as “image, image, image.” The band rebuilt the site. This song is for her.
songs.lesson: Accessibility means people with disabilities can use a system. That includes text alternatives for images so screen readers can describe them, captions for audio, enough color contrast and never relying on color alone, everything usable from a keyboard, and clear structure. Guidelines like WCAG spell it out. Accessible design usually helps everyone, like curb cuts built for wheelchairs that help strollers and suitcases too.

songs.title: Dark Pattern

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The box was checked already and I didn’t see it there,
The button to say no was small and grey and hiding where?
Easy to sign up for and impossible to leave,
A design that works against you is a design made to deceive!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Dark pattern! (Tricked into yes!)
Dark pattern! (Guilt in the mess!)
Usability turned upside down to work against your will,
Dark pattern, dark pattern, and the trick is working still!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: No thanks, I like paying full price, says the guilty little link,
A countdown clock that never ends, to rush you so you won’t think.
The skills that make it easy can be used to make it hard,
Design is a responsibility, so keep it on your guard!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Who does it serve? (The user?)
Who does it serve? (Or the abuser?)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s solo keeps offering a melody that sounds like it’s about to resolve, then leads into a dead end. Every time the band tries to follow it out, there’s another detour. It is deliberately unpleasant.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Dark pattern! (Tricked into yes!)
Dark pattern! (Guilt in the mess!)
Usability turned upside down to work against your will,
Dark pattern, dark pattern, and the trick is working still!

songs.note: The label wanted the mailing-list box pre-checked and the unsubscribe link hidden. The band refused and wrote this instead. The name “dark pattern” came three years later; the tricks were already everywhere.
songs.lesson: Dark patterns are designs that trick people into things they didn’t mean to do: pre-checked boxes, cancellation hidden away, guilt-trip buttons like “No thanks, I like paying full price,” and fake countdown timers. They use what designers know about people against them. Ethical design serves the user’s real interests. The term was coined by Harry Brignull in 2010.

songs.title: Undo

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I made a mistake and I deleted it all,
My finger slipped, and I heard it fall.
But there’s a button in the corner and it takes me back in time,
Undo, and the world is mine!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Undo! (Take it back!)
Undo! (Back on track!)
Let me try and let me fail and let me find my way,
Undo, undo, and I’ll be brave today!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Ask before the thing that can’t be undone, but not for every small,
A warning that appears for everything is no warning at all.
Prevent the slips before they happen, make the safe way the default,
And when they happen anyway, let them back without a fault!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Are you sure? (Every time?)
Then I’m never sure! (Make it fine!)
Just let me undo! (Undo!)

parts.label: Rewind: full band
parts.desc: Midway through the solo, the whole band plays a deliberately wrong chord. Then everything rewinds, with the tape effect audible, back two bars, and they play it again, right. Nobody is punished for the mistake. That’s the point.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Undo! (Take it back!)
Undo! (Back on track!)
Let me try and let me fail and let me find my way,
Undo, undo, and I’ll be brave today!

songs.note: The first pressing of this album came in packaging nobody could open. The band undid it, and the second pressing has a tab that says “pull here.”
songs.lesson: Good design prevents errors before they happen, with constraints and safe defaults, and asks for confirmation only before actions that can’t be reversed, because people stop reading “are you sure?” boxes that appear for everything. It also makes recovery easy: undo lets people explore without fear. Two of Nielsen’s heuristics are error prevention and user control and freedom.
